preamble: Depalatalization of [dʲ] to plain [d] removes the secondary palatal articulation. The clearest case is Ukrainian: consonants that had become soft before front vowels in the East Slavic dialects hardened before original *e and *i, so Ukrainian has plain [d] in день [dɛnʲ] 'day' and водити [wɔˈdɪte] 'to lead' where Russian keeps [dʲ] (день [dʲenʲ], водить [vɐˈdʲitʲ]). Galinskaya (2024) dates this hardening after the common East Slavic secondary softening, and Rubach (2005) treats it as an active depalatalization before [ɛ]. Other Slavic languages with hard [d] before /e/ (Czech den, Bulgarian ден [dɛn]) are not listed because the earlier palatalized stage could not be verified for them.

examples.from: Old East Slavic дьнь (dĭnĭ) 'day' (< Proto-Slavic *dьnь), soft [dʲ] before the front yer (cf. Russian день [dʲenʲ])
examples.note: Ukrainian consonants are hard before /e/; Rubach (2005) analyses a depalatalization process applying before [ɛ] that makes o-fronting opaque.

examples.from: Old East Slavic водити (voditi) 'to lead' (< Proto-Slavic *voditi), soft [dʲ] before и (cf. Russian водить [vɐˈdʲitʲ])
examples.note: Before original *i (Ukrainian и [ɪ]) consonants also hardened; Galinskaya (2024) shows the hardening followed the earlier East Slavic secondary softening.

sources: Rubach, J. (2005). Mid vowel fronting in Ukrainian. Phonology 22(1), 1-36. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0952675705000424
Galinskaya, E. A. (2024). Relative chronology in the language history. Litera 11, 397-407. https://doi.org/10.25136/2409-8698.2024.11.72257
